crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
children.blurb: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance is a structured review of how AI tools and models are introduced, used, and controlled across finance functions such as accounting, treasury, FP&A, credit, and financial reporting.

children.name: Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models
children.blurb: Keeping financial data out of public models covers the controls and practices that stop sensitive financial information from being entered into, retained by, or used to train AI services that are open to the public.

children.name: Model Risk and Bias Testing
children.blurb: Model risk and bias testing covers the controls used to find, measure and limit harm from models that make or inform financial decisions.

children.name: Mapping Financial AI to the Rules
children.blurb: Mapping financial AI to the rules means connecting each AI system used in finance to the laws, regulations, supervisory expectations and internal policies that apply to it.

children.name: Local and Air-Gapped Deployment
children.blurb: Local and air-gapped deployment means running AI models and supporting systems entirely on an organization's own hardware and network, with no connection to external cloud services or the public internet.

sections.body: This field covers how finance teams govern AI systems that touch money, reporting, client data and controls. In practice AI is used to draft reconciliations, flag anomalies, summarize contracts, score credit, and automate parts of audit and tax work. The governance work is about enablement audits that check whether a tool is allowed, who approved it, what data it can see, and how its output is reviewed. Data leakage is a live concern because staff paste ledger extracts, client identifiers, or deal terms into public models. Model risk and bias testing asks whether a model's outputs are stable, explainable, and fair enough for the decision it supports. Regulatory mapping turns broad rules into specific controls, evidence, and reporting lines.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are solved in narrow ways: access controls, data loss prevention, and audit logs are mature in many firms, and local deployment can keep sensitive data inside a controlled environment. What is not solved is the gap between a model passing a test and a model behaving well in production across messy financial data. Bias testing in finance is still uneven because fairness depends on the decision, the population, and the legal context. Regulatory mapping is fragmented across jurisdictions, and rules change faster than many control libraries. The atlas tracks 219 compliance and regulation pages, which reflects how much of the work is now about interpretation and evidence rather than model building. Honest limits include vendor opacity, weak model documentation, and the difficulty of proving a negative, that no sensitive data leaked.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages in this section form a sequence from permission to protection to proof, and together they answer the governance question that runs through The AI Accountant, not just whether AI can do a task, but whether the firm can explain and defend how it did so. The AI Enablement Audit in Finance is the starting point for a reader who needs to know how a tool gets approved and reviewed before it touches financial work. Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models goes deeper into leakage risks and the controls that keep client and ledger data away from external services. Model Risk and Bias Testing covers the testing, documentation, and monitoring that a model needs after it is allowed into use. Mapping Financial AI to the Rules connects those controls to specific regulatory obligations and evidence requests. Local and Air-Gapped Deployment is for readers who need to understand when a model must run inside a firm's own environment rather than in a public cloud.
